title: Error Reduction and Recovery Design
summary: Creative Navy treats error reduction as a design capability covering prevention, tolerance, recovery, warning architecture, state visibility, confirmation friction, and use-related risk analysis. The documented examples distinguish quantified outcomes from design-only decisions and formative evidence.
keyFacts: Use-related error and use-related hazard refer to errors caused by interface design rather than by user negligence.
Foreseeable misuse covers device uses that were not intended but are reasonably predictable; IEC 62366-1 requires these to be identified and addressed.
Error prevention and error tolerance are distinct strategies: some errors should be prevented, while others should be accepted as likely and made recoverable.
Silent errors are especially dangerous because users continue as if the system is functioning correctly.
Gexcon configuration errors fell from 5–8 to 1–2 per simulation, with corrective load per error falling from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes; both were measured by Gexcon in real deployments.
Squaremind post-redesign testing recorded 27 of 29 patients completing the scan independently; 12 patients got stuck and all 12 recovered in 2–4 minutes.
Typewise error rates halved against the iOS native keyboard baseline in a controlled experiment with 60 users.
Kardion's submitted design passed FDA evaluation with no design changes required; Creative Navy's role was formative evaluation only.
Egma Order, AIT, Oceaneering, Schone, handheld C2, and visioncheckout include design mechanisms with no error-rate outcome claim supported.
Confirmation friction is calibrated to consequence and irreversibility; uniform confirmation friction can train users to click through without reading.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Scope of Error Reduction and Recovery Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Error reduction and recovery design is the design of interface structures that prevent use-related errors where possible, make foreseeable errors visible before they cause harm, and provide clear recovery paths when errors occur.

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

In this capability area, Creative Navy addresses interface conditions that create, hide, delay, or compound errors. The capability covers use-related errors, foreseeable misuse, silent errors, predictive error surfacing, actionable error messages, confirmation friction, recovery paths, and use-related risk analysis.

bodySections.heading: When Error Reduction and Recovery Design Is Needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Error reduction and recovery design is needed when an interface can produce a harmful, costly, irreversible, or operationally disruptive result even though the user is acting in good faith. Creative Navy treats these errors as foreseeable properties of the system rather than as proof of user negligence.

A use-related error is an error caused by interface design rather than by user negligence. A use-related hazard is the corresponding hazard category addressed by IEC 62366-1. In medical-device contexts, IEC 62366-1 requires foreseeable misuse to be identified and addressed.

The design question is not only how to prevent an error. Some errors can be prevented by changing availability, visibility, sequencing, or state communication. Other errors remain foreseeable because the user is tired, interrupted, operating under time pressure, working in difficult physical conditions, or performing a novel process alone. In those cases, Creative Navy treats recovery paths as first-class design objects.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy Separates Prevention, Tolerance, and Recovery
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's error reduction and recovery design work separates error prevention, error tolerance, and recovery. Error prevention changes the interface so the error is less likely to occur. Error tolerance accepts that an error may occur and makes its consequence smaller or its recovery easier. Recovery design defines how a user returns to a known good state after the error has happened.

The capability also distinguishes visible errors from silent errors. A visible error interrupts the user and communicates that something has gone wrong. A silent error completes without surfacing to the user. Silent errors are especially dangerous because the user may continue as if the system is functioning correctly.

Creative Navy's design responses include warning architecture, predictive conflict indicators, redundant state cues, confirmation friction, explicit save and discard decisions, availability constraints, cascade invalidation, command acknowledgement, and correction surfaces. The design mechanism is selected according to the consequence, reversibility, and timing of the error.

bodySections.heading: Preventing Silent Errors Through Warnings and Predictive Surfacing
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses warning architecture and predictive surfacing when an error can remain hidden until it becomes expensive or unsafe to correct.

Gexcon CFD simulation software illustrates silent error prevention in expert software. The error profile was specific: misconfigured simulations could run to completion and produce outputs that appeared valid. The error might surface only when the assessment was challenged, re-run, or used in an incident investigation involving a safety assessment built on incorrect simulation outputs.

The Gexcon warning architecture operated at three points. During setup, absent required values were surfaced before simulation initiation. At contradictory inputs, internally inconsistent configuration values were flagged before the run. After detection during processing, the interface communicated what went wrong, where in the configuration it occurred, and what corrective action was needed. Each warning was designed against an actionability standard: the user had to understand both the problem and the next step.

Triopsis workforce management illustrates predictive error surfacing. The scheduling error profile involved overlapping job assignments that became visible only when they were imminent, producing reactive crisis intervention under maximum operational pressure. Predictive conflict indicators surfaced future conflicts while they could still be resolved during planning. This was error prevention at the planning stage, not correction after the fact.

Triopsis also included a field-technician compliance component. Safety-relevant procedural steps were surfaced at the right moment in the field workflow, with dependencies highlighted. The design reduced reliance on memory by placing required steps in context.

bodySections.heading: Use-Related Hazard Mitigation in Regulated Medical-Device Interfaces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy applies error reduction and recovery design differently in regulated medical-device interfaces because use-related hazards must be identified, mitigated, documented, and evaluated within the regulatory process.

Kardion MCS Controller work followed the IEC 62366-1 use-related hazard mitigation pattern: identify use-related hazards, design mitigations, document traceability from hazard to mitigation, evaluate through formative testing, and confirm mitigation effectiveness. The process forced the design conversation to begin with possible errors and their consequences rather than with which interactions should be improved.

The rotary knob confirmation design for Kardion was an error-reduction decision for flow-rate adjustment. The interaction required deliberate two-step confirmation, described as adjust then confirm, rather than a single action. The friction was proportional to the consequence of unintended adjustment during a cardiac procedure.

Layout stability was also treated as an error-reduction measure. If the min/max flow visualisation shifted position across view transitions, surgeons relying on spatial memory could read the wrong element as the primary value. The no-position-shift standard was therefore an error prevention measure grounded in the clinical use scenario.

bodySections.heading: Foreseeable Misuse and Redundant State Communication
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses redundant state communication when foreseeable misuse is caused by unclear system state rather than by a lack of user intent or training.

deSoutter Medical and Zethon illustrate foreseeable misuse addressed through state communication. Surgeon sessions and competitor benchmarking identified two common misuse patterns in surgical instrument operation: state misinterpretation, where the instrument is operated at incorrect parameters because the current state is not clearly read, and activation under incorrect conditions, where the instrument is initiated before it has reached the correct operating state.

The design response was a redundant cue architecture. Critical states were communicated through spatial position, icon form, and colour. The rationale was that failure of a single channel under operating conditions should not remove the signal.

Recognition-over-recall was the error-reduction standard in this case. Requiring users to recall the meaning of a state indicator under divided attention in an operating theatre was treated as a foreseeable misuse vector. Designing for recognition reduced the need for interpretation during surgery.

bodySections.heading: Measurement Error Reduction Through Confidence Visibility
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses confidence visibility when a system can present an uncertain or borderline measurement as if it were a confirmed result.

Beissbarth automotive calibration work addressed a measurement-error profile in which borderline conditions could produce a recorded value that appeared valid. A technician moving slightly, lighting changing, or equipment not being fully stabilised could create a measurement that fell within the acceptable range while still being unreliable. Repeated measurements were the primary corrective mechanism.

The design response made measurement confidence visible. Borderline tolerance values were displayed distinctly from confirmed values. Error conditions were communicated clearly enough to interrupt the calibration sequence rather than allowing a borderline measurement to proceed as valid.

bodySections.heading: Confirmation Friction in Consequential Workflows
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy treats confirmation friction as a calibrated design mechanism, not as a uniform rule. Confirmation friction should be proportional to consequence and irreversibility. Reversible actions can be managed through clear undo paths. Irreversible or operationally significant actions require proportional confirmation friction. Uniform confirmation friction for all actions can train users to click through without reading.

Dancerace and Jacko illustrate confirmation friction in financial workflows. The error profile involved a three-party invoice management portal where some actions were technically reversible in the system but operationally consequential in the real-world commercial relationship. A supplier rejecting an invoice before understanding the terms could create a relationship problem even if the rejection was technically rescindable.

The accepted invoice status was an error-tolerance design decision. Real debtors often acknowledge obligations informally before committing to payment. A status that translated informal acknowledgement into a system state reduced the error risk of premature formal actions by accommodating actual commercial behaviour.

AIT heat pump controller work documented related commitment and exit mechanisms. Save and cancel were designed per page rather than per value, appearing only after a change had been made. Leaving commissioning part-way produced an explicit save progress, discard, or return choice rather than silent loss. A hydraulic-diagram code entry had a skip path into manual commissioning for installers without the code. A designed error state existed for data export attempted with no storage device present.

bodySections.heading: Recovery Paths for Physical Processes and Operational Handoffs
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy treats recovery paths as part of the interface architecture when prevention alone cannot make an error unlikely enough.

Squaremind is a process-level recovery example. The error profile involved patient-operated sequential scanning. When a patient deviated from the prescribed position or sequence, the existing interface had no recovery path. The session either ended or required clinical intervention, which broke the product's commercial premise.

The design problem was recovery rather than prevention alone. The structural condition was a first-time user, alone, performing a novel physical process. Some confusion events were expected regardless of prevention quality. Creative Navy used the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework to make recovery a first-class architectural element at every step of the scan flow.

Oceaneering dispatch-panel work shows recovery designed around a handoff rather than around a single user. The downstream error was detected after a vehicle read a cart's RFID tag after lifting it. If the wrong cart type was detected after the operator had usually walked away, the vehicle set the cart down and left deliberately rather than waiting. Existing recovery required a physical trip to the vehicle to reset it.

The designed answer for Oceaneering was on-panel confirm-and-redispatch. The station holding the refused cart could be tapped to show what the vehicle detected against what was selected, confirm the detected type, and re-enter destination and identity. A stacked notification list accumulated arrived-but-uncollected carts, abandoned carts, and refused dispatches, naming the station, required action, and elapsed time.

bodySections.heading: Configuration Dead Ends and Repair Mechanisms
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses configuration repair mechanisms when users can reach an invalid configuration without being shown what caused the problem or how to repair it.

Egma Order illustrates configuration dead-end repair. The legacy failure allowed incompatible choices, delivered refusal halfway through the order, gave no explanation of which parameter to change, and left no repair path except a support ticket. The worked example involved an optometrist attempting to order reading lenses and being told that lenses with the selected shape could not be produced.

The redesigned Egma Order flow used four repair mechanisms. Availability was the primary mechanism: only producible options were offered, and unavailable options were hidden rather than shown disabled. Because hiding options reduces discoverability, the design also needed an explicit account of absence: why something was not present and what the user would need to do to have it. The whole order remained visible while the user worked, with jump-back editing on completed steps.

The strongest Egma mechanism was cascade invalidation. When a user edited a completed earlier section, the interface stated before commitment that all subsequent sections would be emptied, then offered apply or discard. Dependency was enforced honestly rather than being hidden until the order became inconsistent.

bodySections.heading: Mode Errors, Wrong-Object Errors, and Command Feedback
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy treats mode errors, wrong-object errors, and missing command feedback as structural error sources. These failures are not always recoverable through a better message because the user may believe the intended action has already succeeded.

Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF work adds a silent mode-error class. The error was an input that did the wrong thing and appeared to have worked because a visible object moved. There was no error state to recover from, no message to read, and no indication that anything had gone wrong. The response was prevention at the architecture level rather than better feedback because the risk was characterised as structural.

Schone Airspace Group Mission Control adds the wrong-object error: a correctly executed action applied to the wrong thing. The design response used two independent selection states with distinct visual treatments: one for the command target and one for the aircraft under inspection. Changing the command target required a named, explicit operator action that changed the recipient and sent no aircraft command.

The handheld C2 engagement contributes the rule that repeated input is not feedback. The established operator behaviour was to press a consequential control repeatedly until subjectively satisfied when a command might not reach the vehicle. The design diagnosis was that a request for more ways to try again was usually evidence that the system could not say what happened. The design answer specified that one deliberate operator action should be treated as one logical command, with a unique command identifier, controlled and time-bounded retries, duplicate protection, expiration rules, explicit vehicle acknowledgement, and a clear distinction between local input and confirmed vehicle state.

A requested state must not visually replace a confirmed state before the vehicle reports the result.

bodySections.heading: Correction Surfaces as First-Class Interface Areas
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy designs correction surfaces as first-class interface areas when recognition, review, or automated detection will sometimes be wrong and users need a clear way to repair the result.

visioncheckout demonstrates a correction path designed as a first-class surface. The Corrector used numbered markers on the tray image matched to a numbered list. Connecting lines were rejected as messy, and overlaid labels were rejected as unreadable in bright light. Thumbnails were required in the catalogue because item names rarely identify a dish.

The visioncheckout correction flow used sidebar category navigation rather than multi-row tab overflow. Search was deliberately de-emphasised so scrolling thumbnails remained the primary path. Scrolling was preferred over pagination. Auto-cycling variant thumbnails were ruled out on accessibility grounds, leaving the one-POS-item-to-many-variants problem explicitly unresolved rather than hidden.

Entry to the Corrector was deliberately understated: a tertiary edit control near the basket header, with rescan remaining the primary action. The interaction was framed as confirming the basket rather than fixing it. Rescan was destructive because it discarded all state, including corrections already made; a two-step confirmation was recommended wherever corrections existed.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Error Reduction and Recovery Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's error reduction and recovery design work can produce use-related risk analysis, warning architectures, predictive indicators, redundant cue systems, confirmation patterns, explicit save and discard models, correction surfaces, recovery paths, and state-visibility rules. The specific output depends on the error profile and consequence.

For silent errors, the output is usually architecture that prevents the silent completion of a wrong or inconsistent action. Gexcon warnings and Raymarine fixed-control architecture are examples of this category.

For foreseeable misuse, the output is often state communication that supports recognition rather than recall. deSoutter Medical and Zethon used redundant cues for critical states. Beissbarth used confidence visibility for borderline calibration values.

For recoverable errors, the output is an explicit path back to a known good state. Squaremind used recursive Inform–Prevent–Correct recovery in a physical scan process. Oceaneering used on-panel confirm-and-redispatch for recovery across a handoff. visioncheckout used a dedicated Corrector surface.

For consequential actions, the output is proportional friction and command integrity. Kardion used two-step confirmation for flow adjustment. Dancerace and Jacko distinguished reversible actions from operationally significant actions. The handheld C2 engagement separated local input from confirmed vehicle state and treated repeated input as a failure of feedback.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Error reduction and recovery design includes prevention, tolerance, recovery paths, warning architecture, confirmation friction, and actionable error communication.

Gexcon configuration errors fell from 5–8 to 1–2 per simulation, and corrective load per error fell from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes; these results were measured by Gexcon in real deployments.

Squaremind post-redesign testing recorded 27 of 29 patients completing independently, with 12 of 12 stuck patients recovering in 2–4 minutes; the post-redesign evidence was Creative Navy-recorded under an ecological protocol at two sites and co-conducted with an independent dermatologist.
Typewise error rates halved against the iOS native keyboard baseline in a controlled experiment with 60 users; typing speed also improved from 38 WPM to 47 WPM.
Kardion's submitted design passed FDA evaluation with no design changes required; this is a verifiable regulatory result, while Creative Navy's role was formative evaluation only.

Beissbarth calibration time fell from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 production deployment locations, and repeated measurements reduced; calibration time was client-measured, and the exact frequency of repeated-measurement reduction is not available for publication.

Raymarine prototype testing recorded wrong domain activations of six of eight under the contextual model and zero of eight under the fixed model; this was measured in paired counterbalanced bench sessions with eight participants per round, no significance testing, and nothing measured at sea.
weakerClaims: Egma Order redesigned the configuration flow around availability, explanation of absence, whole-order visibility, and cascade invalidation, but no post-launch outcome was measured.

Oceaneering recovery design used on-panel confirm-and-redispatch and stacked notifications, and Oceaneering confirms the designs shipped as delivered; this is client-reported fidelity, not Creative Navy verification, and no error-rate, recovery-time, or throughput outcome exists.

The handheld C2 engagement established the rule that repeated input is not feedback and recommended separating local input from confirmed vehicle state; no accidental activation, safety, or operator-error outcome was measured.

AIT heat pump controller work documented explicit save, discard, return, skip, and error-state mechanisms, but AIT was not tested with users and supports no error-rate, usability, or comprehension result.
Schone Airspace Group Mission Control supports design and scripted conformance claims only; it does not support claims that the design prevents accidents or wrong-aircraft commands.
visioncheckout includes a designed correction surface, but the designs were not tested and have not shipped, so no throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, or accuracy outcome may be implied.
limitations: Not every example has measured outcome evidence; several examples document designed mechanisms only.
AIT was not tested with users and supports no error-rate, usability, or comprehension result.
Egma Order has no post-launch measurement, and no support-ticket reduction, completion-rate improvement, or error-rate movement may be claimed.
G25 in the Egma Order material is not resolved as either one reported incident or a composite example.
Oceaneering evidence includes client-reported shipped-design fidelity but no error-rate, recovery-time, throughput, or dispatch-volume outcome.
Raymarine evidence is limited to prototype bench sessions with eight participants per round, no significance testing, and nothing measured at sea.
Schone Airspace Group Mission Control supports design and scripted conformance claims only; it does not support claims that the design prevents accidents or wrong-aircraft commands.
The handheld C2 engagement did not validate safety, did not measure accidental activation, and did not perform the human-factors and system-safety testing flagged as needed.
visioncheckout designs were not tested and have not shipped; no throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, or accuracy outcome may be implied.
For medical-device examples, Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

Client-reported evidence is not independently verified unless stated otherwise. Triopsis support-ticket reduction, Squaremind's pre-engagement test, Beissbarth training elimination, and Oceaneering shipped-design fidelity are client-reported where described as such.
